blocker.summary: r450 corrected r449's framing with a direct live check: 0xFE is NOT uninitialized memory that was never written. A hardware watchpoint on the exact byte (guest 0x173b0038), armed from the very first guest instruction (same technique as r437), fired: 'Old value = 0, New value = 254', written by sub_823830F0, called from sub_821D5F48. Decompiling sub_823830F0 confirms it is a plain generic memset implementation (classic alignment-then-word-then-tail-bytes pattern). So sub_821D5F48 deliberately calls memset(pool, 0xFE, size) right after allocating this pool -- a normal 'poison/sentinel' pattern, not an oversight. The open question shifts upstream again: on real hardware something must overwrite this pool with real data (a real file index/handle) before sub_821CC508 reads it, and in this offline environment that overwrite evidently never happens (the byte was still 0xFE at read time, per r449). Consistent with the whole chain (r441-r449): allocate a pool, mark it pending (STATUS_PENDING=0x103 seen earlier, here memset(0xFE)), then wait for an async operation to populate it -- exactly the shape of a PAC/content-loading pipeline whose trigger or completion never occurs offline. Named for r451: trace what should overwrite this pool after the initial memset(0xFE) -- leave a hardware watchpoint armed longer to confirm definitively there is no second writer at all before the crash, not just none before sub_821CC508's read. The native_vulkan_backend.cpp backlog commit decision (r433/r434/r438) remains the other open, user-dependent thread.
